prompt: Sort each study by the way its design treats time.

cards.text: A fitness chain surveys 800 adults once in March to estimate how many hold a gym membership.
cards.explanation: One sample is drawn and measured once: a single cross-sectional design.

cards.text: A bank surveys a new random sample of 500 adults every quarter to track awareness of its brand.
cards.explanation: Each quarter draws a different sample, and each sample is measured once: a multiple cross-sectional design.

cards.text: The same 2,000 households scan every grocery purchase at home each week for two years.
cards.explanation: The same households report repeatedly over time, as in a panel: a longitudinal design.

cards.text: A streaming service compares viewing habits in two independent samples, one drawn in 2023 and one in 2025.
cards.explanation: Two different samples, each measured once, make a multiple cross-sectional design.

cards.text: A telecom firm contacts the same 600 subscribers every six months to record which provider each one uses.
cards.explanation: Measuring the same individuals repeatedly reveals who switches provider: a longitudinal design.

cards.text: A snack brand asks 300 shoppers once, in one week, how they perceive its packaging.
cards.explanation: One sample is measured at one point in time: a single cross-sectional design.

prompt: Each case describes a decision situation. Name the research design that is appropriate at this stage.

cases.text: A publisher's newsletter subscriptions have stagnated, and no one in the firm can suggest why.
cases.explanation: The problem is ambiguous and little is known about it, so exploratory research is appropriate.

cases.text: A car-sharing firm needs to know the age, income, and trip frequency of its current members before planning a campaign.
cases.explanation: The problem is defined and the decision requires an accurate description of a group: descriptive research.

cases.text: An online retailer must decide whether free shipping on orders above 40 euros would increase the average order value.
cases.explanation: The decision depends on the effect of a specific marketing action, so causal research is appropriate.

cases.text: A hotel group wants to understand what business travellers mean when they describe a stay as 'restful', before it drafts any survey.
cases.explanation: The aim is to define the problem and develop hypotheses, which is the purpose of exploratory research.

cases.text: A beverage firm needs an estimate of the share of households in each region that buy sparkling water every month.
cases.explanation: Estimating the magnitude of a phenomenon in a market is the task of descriptive research.

cases.text: A cereal brand has two package designs and must choose the one that produces higher purchase intention.
cases.explanation: Testing whether a package design changes purchase intention requires manipulating the design: causal research.

prompt: Match each criterion for evaluating secondary data with the concern it addresses.

pairs.match: The report does not state how many people were surveyed or what the response rate was.
pairs.explanation: The sample, the response rate and the questionnaire concern how the data were collected: methodology.

pairs.match: Two industry reports estimate the same market at 1.2 and 1.9 billion euros.
pairs.explanation: Comparing several sources reveals the extent of error in the data: accuracy.

pairs.match: The figures on online grocery shopping were collected before the pandemic.
pairs.explanation: When the data were collected, and whether conditions have changed since, is currency.

pairs.match: A study of sugar consumption was funded by a soft drink industry association.
pairs.explanation: Data collected to support a particular position may be biased: purpose.

pairs.match: One source counts 'young adults' as 18 to 24, another as 18 to 34.
pairs.explanation: How key variables, such as age groups, were defined is the definitions criterion.

pairs.match: The statistic appears on an anonymous blog with no stated author or organization.
pairs.explanation: The expertise, credibility and reputation of the source determine its dependability.

prompt: Each case describes a firm's information need. Name the syndicated service that meets it.

cases.text: A yoghurt brand wants to know whether the same households that tried its new flavor bought it again in the following months.
cases.explanation: Repeat purchase by the same households over time is recorded by a consumer panel.

cases.text: A detergent manufacturer wants weekly unit sales of its brand and its competitors' brands across supermarket chains.
cases.explanation: Sales through retail outlets, from point-of-sale scanner data, come from a retail tracking service.

cases.text: An advertiser wants to know how many viewers aged 25 to 44 watched a sports broadcast in which its commercial appeared.
cases.explanation: The size and composition of a television audience are estimated by a media audience measurement service.

cases.text: A snack firm wants to compare the sales of its products in pharmacies and convenience stores after a competitor's price cut.
cases.explanation: Product sales by type of retail outlet are recorded by a retail tracking service.

cases.text: A publisher selling advertising needs an independent estimate of the audience for its digital video channel.
cases.explanation: Audience size for digital media is estimated by a media audience measurement service.

cases.text: A coffee brand wants to see which brands its former buyers switched to over the past year.
cases.explanation: Following the purchases of the same households over time is the function of a consumer panel.

prompt: Each case describes data used by a firm. Name the type of customer data.

cases.text: An online bookshop analyzes the order histories of its registered customers.
cases.explanation: The firm collected the data directly from its own customers: first-party data.

cases.text: A skincare brand's website asks visitors to complete a skin-type quiz, and uses their answers to recommend products.
cases.explanation: Customers provide the answers intentionally, so they are zero-party data, a subset of first-party data.

cases.text: A car rental firm receives booking data directly from a rail operator under a partnership agreement.
cases.explanation: Another organization's first-party data, obtained directly through a partnership, are second-party data.

cases.text: A furniture retailer buys a list of 'recent home movers' from a data broker that compiles it from many websites.
cases.explanation: The broker has no direct relationship with the consumers and sells aggregated data to many buyers: third-party data.

cases.text: A supermarket records which products members scan with its loyalty app.
cases.explanation: The supermarket collects the records directly from its own customers: first-party data.

cases.text: A streaming service's subscribers select their favorite genres in their profile settings.
cases.explanation: Stated preferences that customers enter intentionally in a profile are zero-party data.

prompt: An AI tool has returned a market-size figure with a citation. Put the researcher's verification steps in order.

steps.text: Locate the original source for the reference, independently of the AI tool.
steps.explanation: Verification begins by finding the source without relying on the tool that cited it.

steps.text: Confirm that the source exists and that its authors, publisher, and date are as stated.
steps.explanation: Once located, the source is checked against the reference, since fabricated references look plausible.

steps.text: Confirm that the cited figure appears in the source.
steps.explanation: A real source may still not contain the figure attributed to it.

steps.text: Examine the context of the figure, including its definitions, sample, and date.
steps.explanation: A summary can omit qualifications, so the figure is read in its original context.

steps.text: Evaluate the source against methodology, accuracy, currency, purpose, definitions, and dependability.
steps.explanation: Finally, the source is judged by the same criteria as any secondary data.
